What changes when the regime applies?

It changes how the conflict is told, because attention moves from the isolated event to the supply program. It changes how the conflict is proved, because opacity becomes part of the legal problem. And it changes how the harm is remedied, because money no longer automatically settles the matter when the harm reaches continuity, intelligibility, functional position, practical trust or permanence.

In each family the harmful mechanism, the evidentiary problem and the required restoration are kept distinct. This does not mean the regime works for almost everything. The three dimensions are connected, but they remain distinct.
Harmful modulation is not to be confused with its proof. The evidentiary difficulty is not to be confused with the harm itself.<1>p. 788</1>
What emerges from the analysis of the models is not, therefore, the conclusion that the IOC would work for almost anything.<1>p. 788</1>

And the way of remedying changes, because the response can no longer be automatically satisfied with pecuniary equivalents whenever the harm reaches continuity, intelligibility, functional position, practical trust or conditions of permanence in enjoyment.<1>p. 788</1>

By keeping distinguishable, in each platform family, the mechanism of harmful modulation, the corresponding evidentiary problem and the rationale of restoration required by the regime, both empty abstraction and casuistic dispersion are avoided.<1>p. 788</1>
Do these pages accuse any company?

Showing the mechanism is not condemning the service. Not every platform reproduces the same problem, and those that do don't do it with the same force. Nor does every technology-mediated relationship fall under consumer protection.
What these pages do is test whether the same questions remain useful when the environment changes. They don't say that a given company is abusive. They say where to look.

The point here is not to gather digital examples under a single heading out of mere technological affinity, nor to suggest that every contemporary platform reproduces, with identical intensity, the same form of vulnerability, opacity or capture of enjoyment<1>p. 755</1>
Not every relationship economically mediated by technology will justify applying the CDC.<1>p. 780</1>
The laboratory of origin
The typology was refined in a laboratory of origin, with an illustrative scope of application. The sections below develop it in the full text.

At the level of illustrative application, the work takes as its privileged <1>locus</1> the ecosystem of products and services of the multinational <2>Riot Games</2>, focusing on the game <3>League of </3> <4>p. 37</4> <5>Legends</5> and its extensions on associated platforms. This scope does not seek to exhaust the diversity of the global interactive entertainment industry, but to offer a field of exemplification in which typical structures of semiotic governance, practices of hypercuratorial anticipation, monetization models based on digital goods and recurring patterns of friction between consumers and supplier become particularly clear.<6>p. 36-37</6>

Who decides what you see in an online store? · Platforms · Lex Plataformae
<1>Who decides what you see in an online store?</1><2>Infrastructure and intermediation IOCs</2>

Online stores, social networks and ad platforms usually say they only bring the parties together, like a neutral town square. In practice, they choose what appears first, what stays hidden, who looks trustworthy, what is comparable and what takes a while to arrive.

In other words, whoever buys or sells doesn't see the market. They see the market through the platform's filters. Rankings, reputation, featured spots and recommendations are not details of the shop window, because they are part of what it delivers and they weigh on expectation, on perceived risk and on choice.
A shop window seen through several stacked lenses, each one hiding or enlarging a part of what is for sale.
How do you prove what the shop window hid?

It isn't enough to look at the product that arrived or the post that vanished. You need to rebuild the whole shop window, with the order of the offers, what was a paid ad and what wasn't, the reviews, the trust badges and the reach of each thing.

The most common mistake is to treat the screen as mere decoration. It is part of what the platform supplies, and the way it highlights and hides weighs on your whole choice, and not only on the purchase that went wrong at the end.
It is not enough to examine the final product acquired or the individual content removed, prioritized or hidden. It is necessary to reconstruct the architecture of the experience.<1>p. 763</1>
This includes, depending on the case, the form of presentation of the offers, the distinction between organic and paid results, the role of reviews and reputations [...]<1>p. 763</1>
The first is the tendency to treat the interface as mere visual support, and not as a constitutive part of the supply.<1>p. 763</1>
What can you ask of whoever organizes the shop window?

The way forward is to insist on duties that cover how the platform organizes things. It is fair to ask whether it was clear what was sponsored, whether the reputation shown could be checked and whether unclear criteria made it harder to compare the offers.
When the same company referees the shop window and also profits from what happens in it, the issue may even reach competition among sellers.
The possible dogmatic consequence, in this environment, tends to gravitate around procedural duties of controllability of interface governance.<1>p. 764</1>

It becomes necessary to examine, in an IOC key, whether there was adequate information about the nature of the intermediation, whether the distinction between organic priority and sponsored priority was materially intelligible, whether the reputation displayed was functionally verifiable [...]<1>p. 764</1>

In more serious cases, especially when the platform acts at once as arbiter of the environment and as an economic agent with a stake in its results, the opacity of the ranking may also intersect with broader abusive practices and carry competition repercussions of its own.<1>p. 764</1>
Why is intermediation not neutral?

The utility does not end with the good, the content or the advertiser at the end of the chain. It is an infrastructure of visibility, reputation, curation, intermediation and logistics. The platform selects, ranks, highlights, hides and reorganizes the way the environment becomes perceptible. Rankings, reputation, featured placement, recommendation and reach modulation are part of the functional utility. On marketplaces, the consumer chooses within a field the platform has already interpreted. On social networks the same mechanism reappears, because the platform manages how content enters the field of perception.
The platform, therefore, produces the perceptible market itself.<1>p. 762</1>
What is offered, in legally relevant terms, is an infrastructure of visibility, reputation, curation, intermediation and logistics<1>p. 761</1>
They select, rank, highlight, hide, bring closer, delay, prioritize and reorganize the way in which the reality of the environment becomes perceptible to the user.<1>p. 761</1>
Rankings, reputation, featured placement, recommendation, prioritization and reach modulation are not peripheral elements.<1>p. 761</1>
The consumer chooses within a field already pre-interpreted by the platform.<1>p. 762</1>
It manages the way in which these contents enter the user's field of perception and how their relevance is socially stabilized.<1>p. 762</1>
What vulnerability does the interface produce?

The asymmetry is not only about how much information there is. It concerns who constitutes the relevant field of the decision. The platform defines what stands out, what is hidden, what seems more trustworthy and what becomes almost invisible. The promise also lies in the implicit intelligibility of the market or of social circulation, and it suffers when opaque or non-auditable criteria govern it.
The consumer faces an asymmetry in the constitution of the relevant field of the decision.<1>p. 763</1>

The platform defines what stands out, what is hidden, what seems more trustworthy, what acquires the appearance of consensus, what emerges as comparable and what becomes practically invisible.<1>p. 763</1>
It also lies in the implicit promise of intelligibility of the market or of social circulation.<1>p. 763</1>
How is the experience reconstructed?

Examining the final product or the removed content is not enough. The presentation of the offers has to be reconstructed, along with the distinction between organic and paid results, reviews and reputations, the integration between visibility and logistics, the signals of trustworthiness and the moderation criteria. On social networks, that means the feed, the recommendation and the reach. On marketplaces, ranking, featured placement, seller rating and sponsorship. The blind spots are treating the interface as visual support, limiting liability to what appears in a clause or in advertising and reducing the dispute to the terminal act.
It is not enough to examine the final product acquired or the individual content removed, prioritized or hidden.<1>p. 763</1>

The examination checks whether there was adequate information about the intermediation, whether the distinction between organic and sponsored priority was intelligible, whether the reputation displayed was verifiable and whether opacity compromised relevant comparability. When the platform is both arbiter of the environment and interested in the results, the issue may intersect with broader abusive practices and with competition repercussions. Open auditability and functional equivalence operate as cross-cutting filters.

Who is in charge of work done through an app? · Platforms · Lex Plataformae
<1>Who is in charge of work done through an app?</1><2>Productivity IOCs under the gig economy</2>

For people who work this way, the app supplies more than a payment per task. It supplies the very environment that makes the work possible, and the app governs that environment. That is why it isn't enough to look at what the contract says about autonomy. You have to look at who actually controls access to demand, how much you can earn and whether you get to stay in the stream of work.
A city map in which the route of a delivery bicycle is drawn by an enormous hand, with rating stars floating over the path.
How do you prove the app's rule changed?

Showing that earnings fell or that the account was blocked once isn't enough. You need to link the loss to the way the app governs the work, with the history of requests, the variations in pay, the alerts, the criteria disclosed or hidden and the records of restriction.
And a drop in earnings isn't always a natural risk of the activity. It may come from a rule change that nobody explained.

It is not enough to demonstrate that there was a reduction in earnings or an isolated block. It is necessary to reconstruct the relationship between the governance mechanism and the functional impact.<1>p. 768</1>

This may involve history of requests, variations in remuneration, internal communications of the app, performance alerts, criteria disclosed or omitted, records of restriction, rating patterns and comparative data on the change in the environment.<1>p. 768</1>
The first is treating the fluctuation of earnings as a pure natural risk of the activity, when it may result from an opaque unilateral reconfiguration of the distribution infrastructure.<1>p. 768</1>
What can you ask for when the app changes the rule?
An active account doesn't prove that nothing changed. The question is whether your place in the app is still equivalent to the one that backed your expectation of earning and of staying on.

When the change hollows out that place, you may be able to demand the records, the reasons for the restrictions, a review of the criteria and the restoration of what was degraded. This doesn't turn everything into a labor matter, but it doesn't let a contract that talks about autonomy end the conversation either.

The legal test cannot be only whether the account remains active. It needs to be whether the partner's functional position in the environment remains substantially equivalent to the one that structured his legitimate expectation of earnings and permanence.<1>p. 767-768</1>

The most adequate institutional response will tend to favor preservation and display of minimum records, duties of verifiable reasoning, review of restriction criteria, intelligibility about relevant parameters of distribution of opportunities and functional restoration of the regime [...]<1>p. 768</1>
[...] does not dissolve the subtype into undifferentiated labor law, but neither does it let itself be neutralized by contractual self-descriptions of formal autonomy.<1>p. 768</1>
What does the platform supply to those who work on it?

A private infrastructure of economic possibility. It organizes access to demand, distribution of requests, predictability of pay, permanence in the productive flow, reputational criteria, prioritization and sanction. The self-description as intermediary and the formal freedom to switch the app on and off do not solve the problem. The examination falls on the supply regime, without automatically reclassifying the relationship under the categories of the employment contract and without reducing it to the dichotomy between autonomy and subordination.
The platform asserts independence at the contractual end and intensifies governance at the operational end.<1>p. 767</1>
The legally relevant question is not only whether the platform describes itself as an intermediary or whether the partner is formally free to switch the app on and off.<1>p. 766</1>

The central point lies not only in asserting algorithmic subordination in the abstract, nor in automatically reclassifying the whole relationship under traditional categories of the employment contract.<1>p. 766</1>
That is why the dogmatic problem cannot be reduced to the simplistic dichotomy between autonomy and subordination.<1>p. 767</1>
What vulnerability does productive dependence add?

Metrics, incentive messages, quality alerts, promotions, acceptance patterns, pricing dynamics and performance notifications work as a private language for governing conduct. The partner depends on these signs to know his own position, the expectation of earnings and the risk of restriction or exclusion. The opacity falls on the material living conditions of those who depend on the environment to work.

Changes in request distribution, pricing, eligibility, incentives or reputational weights may keep the account and the program's name while hollowing out the economic utility. The test cannot be only whether the account remains active. It must be whether the partner's functional position remains substantially equivalent.
Metrics, incentive messages, quality alerts, promotions, acceptance patterns, pricing dynamics and notifications about performance operate as a private language for governing conduct.<1>p. 766</1>
It regulates access to income, minimum predictability of livelihood and the practical possibility of remaining economically active.<1>p. 767</1>

Changes in criteria of request distribution, in pricing parameters, in eligibility rules, in incentive models or in reputational weights may keep the name of the program, the appearance of the partnership and even the formal existence of the account<1>p. 767</1>

When is the harm collective?

It is not enough that many consumers are hit by similar facts. Collective redress is justified when the harmful source is unitary, repeatable and built into the ordinary functioning of the platform. Repeated opacity, persistent absence of history and non-auditable mutability form a defect of regime. This is architecture harm, produced by the design of the supply. The effects are not homogeneous, but the matrix is common.
The harm, thus, is not only to the individual result of consumption. It is to the institutional verifiability of the supply.<1>p. 774</1>
The basis of collective redress, here, does not lie only in the circumstance that many consumers may be hit by similar facts.<1>p. 774</1>
Collective redress is justified when the harmful source remains unitary, repeatable and incorporated into the ordinary functioning of the platform.<1>p. 774</1>
Repeated opacity, persistent absence of history and non-auditable mutability form, together, a defect of regime.<1>p. 774</1>
The impact is not homogeneous in all its effects, but it is common in its matrix.<1>p. 776</1>
What can collective redress impose?

Inhibitory, procedural and analytical measures that reintroduce verifiability, such as preservation of minimum records, verifiable reasoning for relevant sanctions, accessible history of changes and minimum operational criteria for distribution, priority or ranking. Individual protection remains indispensable to repair concrete losses. Treatment that is only atomized tends to monetize episodes without changing the structure and to turn the systemic difficulty of proof into a private failure of dispersed consumers.
Collective redress thus proves particularly suited to imposing inhibitory, procedural and analytical measures capable of reintroducing institutional verifiability into the environment.<1>p. 775</1>

This may involve duties of preservation of minimum records, a requirement of verifiable reasoning for materially relevant sanctions, maintenance of an accessible history of relevant changes, explicit statement of minimum operational criteria of distribution, priority or ranking<1>p. 775</1>
This does not mean abolishing the role of individual protection.<1>p. 775</1>
On the one hand, it monetizes episodes without changing the machine that reproduces them.<1>p. 776</1>

On collective redress under open auditability
Open auditability · The jurist's way · Lex Plataformae
<1>The jurist's way</1>
Open auditability

Open auditability is the minimum threshold of external verifiability that makes it possible to reconstruct what the supplier changed, when, why and with what effect, whenever the change or the sanction significantly affects the enjoyment of an Immaterial Object of Consumption. The requirement arises within the CDC, has a delimited scope and does not yield to secrecy or to technical complexity.
What problem does open auditability solve?

In a continuous digital service, asking whether the platform may change the environment gets you little, because change is part of how the service is provided. The legal problem is to distinguish legitimate mutation from mutation that breaks the balance of the supply, degrades the promised enjoyment or makes the very possibility of control opaque. This last case has a trait of its own, since many disputes arise not from abrupt removal but from gradual alterations, interface changes and visibility adjustments that seem trivial when taken one by one. The consumer keeps the account, keeps seeing the object and keeps accessing the platform, while its usefulness may drop and, with it, the consumer's ability to prove the drop.
In IOCs, mutability exists, but it does not hover above the Law.<1>p. 635</1>

The legal problem, therefore, lies not in finding out whether the platform may alter the environment, but in establishing the criteria by which legitimate mutation is distinguished from the mutation that breaks the balance of the supply, degrades the promised enjoyment or makes opaque the very possibility of control.<1>p. 635</1>

The consumer remains formally “inside” the ecosystem, keeps the account, keeps seeing the object, can keep accessing the platform. Even so, the utility enjoyed may be substantially lowered, and the capacity to prove this lowering may be simultaneously eroded by the very way the environment is administered.<1>p. 635</1>

The difficulty lies in who holds the information. The supplier controls the architecture, the criteria for change, the logs, which are the automatic records of what the system did, the moment of the change and the very means by which it will be perceived. It thus concentrates the power to reconfigure and also the power to be the sole narrator of what happened. The effect appears in two images, that of the supplier who comes to hold the practical monopoly of the real and that of the consumer reduced to a bearer of symptoms, who feels that something important has been lost but cannot show what was lost, how it was lost or why the loss goes beyond the ordinary annoyances of life online.
The supplier comes to hold the practical monopoly of the “real”, and the consumer is reduced to a bearer of symptoms, without a common language that allows comparison and control.<1>p. 473</1>

That is why opacity, in these environments, is not merely a technical feature. It works as an asymmetric distribution of power within the relationship. Whoever controls the criteria, the records, the system's memory and the language in which events can be described also concentrates the capacity to define what will count as demonstrable. Without a verifiable minimum, the conflict tends to become an unequal contest between the consumer's subjective experience and a self-justifying corporate account, and private governance also becomes power over the institutional conditions of proof. The parameter is aimed at this practical immunity.

Whoever controls the criteria for change, the records of what was done, the memory of the system and the language in which these events can be described also concentrates the capacity to define what will be considered demonstrable.<1>p. 728</1>
Without minimum auditability, the conflict tends to be degraded into an unequal confrontation between the consumer's subjective experience and a formally self-justified business version.<1>p. 728</1>
Private governance then ceases to be only a power to modulate enjoyment and also becomes a power to control the institutional conditions of proof.<1>p. 728</1>
Why does neither total transparency nor published information solve the problem?

The debate usually gets stuck between two positions. One holds that any transparency requirement compromises trade secrets, innovation or business autonomy, and the other imagines that effective control requires full disclosure of the platform's inner workings. Both fail, and the clash is a binary theater, because the first turns technical complexity into an alibi and the second confuses legal protection with an invasion of the productive environment. Rejecting both has a practical effect, since making control conditional on total transparency produces paralysis, and accepting mutability as a neutral given normalizes substantial degradation as mere operational variation.

On one side, it is argued that any transparency requirement would compromise trade secrets, innovation or business autonomy. On the other, it is imagined that control would only be effective if there were complete opening of the platform's internal functioning. Both positions are bad. The first turns technical complexity into an alibi for irresponsibility. The second confuses legal protection with total invasion of the productive environment. Open auditability rejects this binary theater.<1>p. 727</1>
The attempt to condition the legal control of opaque ecosystems on total transparency misses the target and produces paralysis.<1>p. 481</1>

The frustration of the enjoyment bundle then tends to present itself as noise, and the legal response oscillates between two equally unproductive extremes: requiring total transparency incompatible with the functioning of the technical-organizational environment or accepting mutability as a neutral given, normalizing substantial degradations as mere operational variation.<1>p. 469</1>

The supplier's usual answer is that the information is already available, in the terms, in cross-references, in the FAQs and in the update history. That is not enough, because information, under the CDC, does not fulfill its function merely by existing somewhere. What matters is whether it helps reconstruct events and make decisions, that is, whether it lets the consumer know what happened and decide what to do. Without that, what remains is documentary staging and performative transparency, in which the consumer knows that something changed but cannot tell what changed, by what criterion, with what practical effect or how to prove the impact.
The change exists, the notice exists, the document exists, the history exists, but the useful reconstruction of the event does not exist.<1>p. 641</1>

Information, under the CDC, does not fulfill its function merely because it exists somewhere, nor because it was deposited in lengthy documents, cross-references, FAQs or update histories that the consumer will hardly locate, understand and connect to the actual impact suffered. What matters is its reconstructive and decisional usefulness.<1>p. 641</1>
Instead of real transparency, there is only a documentary staging of compliance, a situation incompatible with the standard of adequate and conspicuous information required by the CDC<1>p. 640</1>

The contemporary problem, therefore, is not only the absence of information but its strategic organization. The platform may flood the consumer with announcements, changelogs, which are the public records of changes, on-screen notices, policies and FAQs, and still keep effective control over the intelligibility of what matters. Combined with the technical concentration of records, this mutability produces a private evidentiary fortress.
This effect is all the more important because the contemporary problem is not only absence of information, but strategic organization of information.<1>p. 646</1>

The platform may flood the consumer with announcements, changelogs, banners, dialog boxes, policies, disclaimers and FAQs, and still preserve for itself the effective monopoly over the intelligibility of what matters.<1>p. 646</1>
Without this, the mutability of the service and the technical concentration of records produce, together, a kind of private evidentiary fortress.<1>p. 646</1>

Nor do the two usual doctrinal escape routes help. The civil-law ontology of ownership of the digital good is too narrow for governed consumption, and the microscopic analysis of isolated clauses assumes that the platform produces unlawfulness only through badly drafted contract wording. The focus shifts to the architecture of the supply and to the material controllability of its mutations.

In governed ecosystems, the relevant unlawful act often lies not in a heroically villainous clause, but in the way the environment changes, justifies itself poorly, erases traces and preserves only the formal appearance of continuity.<1>p. 639</1>

It is no longer necessary to reduce the conflict to a civil-law ontology of ownership of the digital good, which would be narrow for governed consumption. Nor is there a need to remain tied to the microscopic analysis of isolated clauses, as if the platform only produced unlawfulness through badly drafted contractual sentences. The focus comes to fall on the architecture of the supply and on the material controllability of its mutations.<1>p. 639</1>
Is open auditability a new right?

No, and the distinction matters for anyone grounding a claim. Open auditability is neither an autonomous statutory right nor a body foreign to the consumer protection microsystem. It is an internal development of three things the system already has, the duty to inform, objective good faith and the facilitation of the consumer's defense. Whether called an operator, a standard or a parameter, it always designates a requirement that the interpreter applies to the case, one of technically qualified transparency that institutions can actually use. It can be demanded whenever the supplier makes relevant changes, imposes sanctions or carries out reconfigurations capable of reaching the core of enjoyment.

A standard of minimum verifiability, compatible with the protection of software and of business secrecy, but incompatible with the opaque shielding of execution; a development of the duty to inform, of objective good faith and of the facilitation of the consumer's defense; a criterion for reducing evidentiary and informational asymmetry; and an institutional condition for relevant mutations of the IOC to cease being accepted as accomplished facts narrated only by the supplier itself.<1>p. 648</1>

Open auditability designates, in continuous digital services, a standard of technically qualified and institutionally usable transparency, enforceable whenever the supplier makes relevant changes, sanctions or reconfigurations capable of reaching the core of enjoyment of the Immaterial Object of Consumption.<1>p. 639-640</1>

The first support is the duty to inform. The manual by Benjamin, Marques and Bessa requires correct, clear, precise and conspicuous information, notes the need for the consumer to be able to review the contract in advance and recalls that information is part of the contractual content and, when it fails, may amount to a quality defect. Ricardo Morishita Wada adds that leaving the time for performance to the supplier's sole determination strips the consumer of the capacity for control, and Bruno Miragem treats the duty to inform as a duty of clarification, which the supplier itself bears the burden of proving it fulfilled and whose breach may trigger Article 46 of the CDC<1><2>1</2></1>. On this basis rests the step that grounds the category. A supplier who alters central elements of enjoyment without providing an intelligible basis for reconstructing what happened does more than communicate poorly, since it prevents control and worsens the consumer's position in the relationship.
The Manual synthesizes this standard by requiring “correct”, “clear”, “precise” and “conspicuous” information <1>Bessa</1><2>(Benjamin; Marques; Bessa, 2021, [p. 128])</2>.<3>p. 640</3>

In addition, clear and adequate information governs the pre-contractual moment, the conclusion of the contract, the contract itself and the post-contractual moment, affecting “the essence of the deal”, since it is part of the contractual content and, if it fails, may represent a defect in the quality of the product or service offered <1>Bessa</1><2>(Benjamin; Marques; Bessa, 2021, [p. 126])</2>.<3>p. 640</3>

Failing to state the time for performance, or leaving its definition to a later moment under the supplier's exclusive control, places the consumer in a situation of extreme vulnerability, because without an intelligible reconstruction of the way the obligation is performed the consumer loses capacity for control and the supplier comes to dictate unilaterally the rules of the game <1>Wada</1><2>(Wada, 2016, p. 208)</2>.<3>p. 641</3>

Adequate information about the relevant elements of the performance serves as a criterion for assessing the regular exercise of the supplier's contractual freedom; its breach may reveal abusiveness, compromise the quality of consent and even attract Article 46 of the CDC<1><2>1</2></1>. Demonstrating that this duty was effectively fulfilled is an evidentiary burden of the supplier itself <3>Miragem</3><4>(Miragem, 2020, p. 412)</4>.<5>p. 643</5>

If the supplier alters obligations, usage parameters, compatibility conditions or central elements of enjoyment without providing a minimally intelligible basis for reconstructing what occurred, it does not merely communicate poorly. It prevents control.<1>p. 641</1>

The second support is objective good faith during performance. In a digital service, performance is not exhausted in an initial delivery, because the relationship extends through updates, fixes, rebalancing and sanctions, and treating this period as a neutral space would be far too crude. Claudia Lima Marques rejects the idea of an empty space between the birth of the obligation and the satisfaction of the performance and describes the relationship as a continuous whole, with ancillary duties to inform, to cooperate and to act loyally. For her, breaching them amounts to nonperformance, even if only partial. The long-term contract, in turn, rests more on trust and on the maintenance of quality, so the supplier cannot keep all the intelligibility of the process of change to itself and leave the consumer with nothing but the imposed result.

Objective good faith, in relationships of this nature, projects continuous duties of information, cooperation, loyalty and protection of trust, so that the supplier cannot reserve for itself all the intelligibility of the process of mutation of the service and leave the consumer only with the final result already imposed<1>p. 640</1>

Breaching the duty of cooperation and loyalty means nonperformance, even if partial, including when the supplier hinders the consumer's access to their rights <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 236)</2>.<3>p. 641</3>

In relationships of continued performance, the consumer places trust not only in an initial utility, but in the minimally intelligible permanence of the relationship and in the possibility of understanding its relevant changes.<1>p. 645</1>

The third support is the facilitation of defense. Article 6, item VIII, of the CDC<1><2>2</2></1>, according to the manual by Benjamin, Marques and Bessa, is not merely procedural in nature, because it aims at effective protection and redress, and the spirit of the Code is not to place on the vulnerable party the burden of proving elements that belong to the supplier's professional risk. Since the platform concentrates records, histories, enforcement criteria and versions, facilitating the defense and redistributing the burden cease to be occasional instruments and become a condition for the regime to have even minimal effectiveness. Open auditability then works as a technique for reducing informational and evidentiary asymmetry, which puts the conflict back on ground where events can be reconstructed.

The Manual is clear in observing that the right provided for in art. 6, VIII, although it aims to facilitate the consumer's procedural defense, is not merely procedural in nature: it is a substantive right aimed at the effective protection and reparation of the damages suffered <1>Bessa</1><2>(Benjamin; Marques; Bessa, 2021, [p. 146])</2>.<3>p. 642</3>

The facilitation of defense and the redistribution of the burden of proof cease to be occasional instruments and become a condition of minimum effectiveness of the protective regime itself.<1>p. 642</1>
Open auditability, at this point, works as a technique for reducing informational and evidentiary asymmetry.<1>p. 642</1>

The systematic consequence is that the lack of auditability does not open an autonomous path of imputation. Quality defect, abusive practice and abusive clause remain the three doors into the CDC, the subject of the chapter on the unlawful act of architecture. The absence of auditability does not create a fourth door but reinforces any of them, because opacity may intensify the imputation for abusive practice, aggravate the reading of the clause that shields arbitrariness and weaken the defense that there was merely a legitimate adaptation. It is a legal technology of controllability, and what it makes possible is a discussion of defect, inadequacy, abusiveness and breach of the duty to inform on a reconstructible basis.
The same hypothesis may simultaneously reveal a quality defect, an abusive practice and an abusive clause, and in borderline cases even approach the logic of the safety defect.<1>p. 678</1>
The absence of auditability does not create an autonomous fourth door, but structurally reinforces any of the others.<1>p. 678</1>

When the platform does not preserve minimum trails, does not offer verifiable reasoning, concentrates proof and prevents reconstruction of what it altered or of the reason why it sanctioned, this opacity intensifies the imputation for abusive practice, aggravates the reading of the predisposed clause that shields arbitrariness and weakens the defense that there would have been a mere legitimate adaptation of the performance.<1>p. 678</1>
Open auditability is a legal technology of controllability.<1>p. 645</1>

This allows defect, inadequacy, abusiveness, breach of the duty to inform and breach of trust to be discussed on a reconstructible basis, and not in a crude confrontation between corporate narrative and the consumer's subjective feeling.<1>p. 645</1>
Why can the Law control without seeing everything?

Control does not depend on full transparency, and the support comes from legal theory. Humberto Ávila proposes shifting the focus from security of meaning to security of criteria, with prior parameters for addressing later interpretive problems, and distinguishes security from transparency. Transparency has its core in information, while security seeks argumentative rationality and the control of arbitrariness. The question is then no longer how to open the black box all the way down but how to define controllable criteria that turn modulations, that is, the continuous changes in the conditions of the service, into legally decidable alternatives.

It is in this sense that Humberto Ávila formulates an explicit turn by arguing that one should shift the focus from security of meaning to security of criteria, in order to provide, in advance, prior and abstract parameters to face later and concrete interpretive problems <1>Ávila</1><2>(Ávila, 2011, p. 71)</2>.<3>p. 472</3>

The question is not to open the black box all the way down, but to define prior and controllable criteria that make it possible to turn technically opaque modulations into legally decidable alternatives, without reducing control to automatic deference to complexity.<1>p. 472</1>

Tércio Sampaio Ferraz Jr. completes the argument through the function of legal dogmatics. He presents it as a technology geared to action, which carves out what can be handled in the form of a decision, and recalls that the actual legal decision works with incomplete information and that its immediate purpose is to absorb insecurity, turning undecidable incompatibilities into decidable alternatives. On the platform, opacity tends to make the dispute endless, because there is always some technical backstage that could explain the effect. A minimum threshold works as a mechanism of finitude, since it organizes the debate around elements that can be argued in adversarial proceedings.
The Law does not need to see everything in order to control.<1>p. 473</1>

In platform-governed consumption, structural opacity tends to push the dispute toward endlessness, because there always remains a technical “behind” that could explain the effect. A minimum threshold of auditability operates as a mechanism of finitude, organizing the debate around elements that are reconstructible and discussable under adversarial proceedings, without the fiction of total transparency.<1>p. 474</1>

Ferraz Jr. formulates the point in terms that serve as a rule of method: “absorption of insecurity” means that the act of deciding “transforms undecidable incompatibilities into decidable alternatives”, without promising to eliminate the conflict, but converting it into something treatable <1>Jr.</1><2>(Ferraz Jr., 2003, [p. 312])</2>.<3>p. 481</3>

Julie E. Cohen and Eros Roberto Grau explain why this control is justified. Cohen describes dominant platforms as agents that produce a territory of their own, made of protocols, data flows and algorithms, and argues that any meaningful control of this environment depends on a baseline level of information about what those mechanisms do. Grau, discussing how the legal rule takes shape in Duguit, links the legal norm to socially organized sanction and observes that the market establishes an order of its own making. On platforms, the sanction takes the form of suspension, banning, reduced visibility and blocked features, carried out through architecture and internal procedures. When this operates as a pattern, the demand for auditability is no longer a matter of transparency for appearance's sake and becomes a minimum requirement for subjecting private coercion to rational control.

Julie E. Cohen describes this power by treating dominant platforms as agents capable of producing and controlling a kind of territory of their own, which is not physical, but is built by protocols, data flows and algorithms, and which presents itself to the user as a space demarcated and protected by guarded borders <1>Cohen</1><2>(Cohen, 2019, p. 235)</2>.<3>p. 474</3>

Discussing the formation of the legal rule from Duguit, Grau indicates that a social norm becomes a legal norm when the mass of consciences understands that the sanction can be “socially organized” <1>Grau</1><2>(Grau, 2008, p. 73)</2>.<3>p. 476</3>
The same intuition appears when Grau observes that the market posits its legal order by establishing an order produced by it <1>Grau</1><2>(Grau, 2008, p. 326)</2>.<3>p. 476</3>

Cohen herself formulates the need for this threshold by arguing that algorithms and protocols classify subjects, shape informational flows and authorize or deny access to network resources, so that any meaningful control of the environment depends on a baseline level of information about what these mechanisms do <1>Cohen</1><2>(Cohen, 2012, [p. 189])</2>.<3>p. 475</3>

On platforms, the sanction materializes in suspension, banning, lowering of visibility, blocking of features, restrictions on participation and multiple forms of automated or hybrid sanction, executed by architecture and by internal procedures.<1>p. 476</1>
The demand for auditability is not an aesthetic transparency agenda, but a minimum requirement for subjecting private coercion to rational control.<1>p. 476</1>
What needs to be auditable?

The trigger is a relevant effect on enjoyment, and it is strictly delimited so that the parameter does not slide into maximalism. The parameter's proper field begins when the change, the unilateral modulation, the removal, the migration, the nerf, which is the adjustment that reduces an item's power or usefulness, the discontinuation, the reconfiguration of a rule or of the interface, or the sanction applied to the user affects enjoyment in a relevant way. Relevance may show up in access and permanence, in the functional integrity of the object, in the promised equivalences, in the object's symbolic position in the ecosystem or in the consumer's conditions for proving and challenging. The central point is that the change must be capable of lowering enjoyment, frustrating a legitimate expectation or abusively concentrating in the supplier's hands the intelligibility of what happened.

Its proper field begins when the change, the unilateral modulation, the suppression, the migration, the nerf, the discontinuation, the reconfiguration of a rule or of the interface, or even the sanction applied to the user, affects enjoyment in a relevant way.<1>p. 642</1>

The central point is that the change must be capable of lowering enjoyment, frustrating legitimate expectation or abusively concentrating the intelligibility of what occurred in the supplier's hands.<1>p. 642</1>

The requirement is selective and functional, because it falls on what makes the dispute decidable. It covers relevant changes in access rules, reconfigurations with functional impact, version changes that affect usefulness or performance, sanctions on permanence or visibility, ordinary modulations of the environment and decision criteria with material effects on enjoyment. None of this may remain in a zone where nothing can be demonstrated, shielded by the mere claim of technical complexity. The mention of ordinary modulations does not dispense with the trigger, because what these cases share is legal interference with enjoyment, and only what interferes with it becomes subject to control.
What must be auditable is not everything, but what matters to make the dispute decidable.<1>p. 727</1>

Relevant changes in access rules, reconfigurations with functional impact, version changes that affect utility or performance, sanctions falling on permanence or visibility, ordinary modulations of the environment and decision criteria with material repercussion on enjoyment cannot remain in a zone of non-demonstration protected by the mere claim of technicality.<1>p. 727</1>
What is required is not to strip the whole system bare, but to make controllable, to a sufficient threshold, what legally interferes with enjoyment.<1>p. 727</1>

Once the trigger is present, the minimum content is more modest than the caricature of total disclosure and more robust than corporate self-justification. It comprises an intelligible record of what was changed and when, a minimum technical justification, understood as the declared rationale and the stated objective, a description of the relevant impacts on enjoyment and on the object's parameters, the preservation of verifiable trails, such as histories of relevant versions and minimum logs of events, transactions or changes, and, in enforcement cases, that is, sanctions applied by the platform itself, minimally reconstructible criteria for the measure. Added to this is the possibility of verification by qualified third parties, including consumer protection bodies, expert examination or judicial review.

The supplier must make available, in an institutionally useful way, an intelligible record of what was changed and of the moment of the change; a minimum technical justification, that is, the declared rationale and the stated objective for the change; a description of the relevant impacts on enjoyment and on the parameters of the IOC; preservation of verifiable trails, such as histories of relevant versions, minimum logs of events, transactions or changes; and, in enforcement cases, minimally reconstructible criteria for the sanction applied.<1>p. 643</1>

In addition, there must be a possibility of verification by qualified third parties, including by protection bodies, expert examination or judicial review, without the regime of technical secrecy being used as an absolute screen against any scrutiny<1>p. 643</1>

The same requirement appears in another formulation, as a standard of verifiable reasoning. When the platform changes access rules, reconfigures features or imposes sanctions that substantially affect utility, it cannot simply invoke generalities, and the reasoning has four elements. It identifies the act and when its effects take hold, indicates the functional impact, sets out the operational reasons with their purpose and criteria of application, and points to the means of challenge and review. The two lists do not fully coincide, and reading them together helps the lawyer, because the first adds the trails and the qualified third party, and the second adds the route for challenge.

This minimum threshold can be described as identifying the act of modulation and the timing of its effects, indicating the functional impact on practical dimensions of enjoyment, setting out the operational reasons with their purpose and criteria of application, and indicating the means of challenge and review.<1>p. 475-476</1>

The effect is to move the dispute from an untellable narrative to a verifiable reconstruction, without turning every adjustment into litigation and without demanding an exhaustive explanation.<1>p. 476</1>

Sufficiency is measured functionally. Intelligibility must be enough to identify the relevant change, relate it to the promised enjoyment, check whether the justification is compatible with the legal regime and establish whether the sanction, change or modulation met minimum standards of predictability, proportionality and contestability. It is addressed to consumer protection bodies, the courts, experts and, to some extent, consumers themselves, who need not understand the system but do need to locate what was promised, what was delivered and what was reconfigured afterward.

The point is to ensure enough verifiable elements to locate what was promised, what was actually delivered and what was later reconfigured through acts of maintenance, curation, updating, enforcement and administration of the conditions of access and use.<1>p. 473</1>
What can be gathered before asking the supplier for anything?

A discipline of reconstruction can guide the opening steps of the lawyer's work. In moving from the game to general parameters, the reconstruction must be verifiable through elements attributable to the supplier and publicly retrievable, such as update records, stated reasons for changes, access policies and internal sanction criteria, which keeps individual experiences from being mistaken for proof. Public statements by users play a subsidiary role, as a symptomatic record of recurring frictions, and do not replace official documents, interface records, court cases or decisions.

Being guided by frictions and sector evidence does not license subjectivism, because analytical discipline comes from stating the conceptual lenses explicitly in advance and from requiring a verifiable reconstruction through elements attributable to the supplier and publicly retrievable, among them update records, declared rationales for change, access policies and internal sanction criteria.<1>p. 498-499</1>

On the contrary, it reorganizes it as a commitment to criteria for selecting evidence and to a theoretical regulation of what counts as relevant observation, reducing confirmation bias and preventing individual experiences from being mistaken for proof.<1>p. 499</1>
This material is not mobilized as autonomous proof of the supplier's institutional conduct, nor as a substitute for official documents, interface records, lawsuits or decisions.<1>p. 66</1>

The material to which the parameter applies is concrete. It includes change communications, the history of relevant versions, confirmation screens, change notices, transaction records and minimum documentation of the supply flow. Where risk is manufactured and loss is a permanent threat, the minimum signal of proof appears in the policies applied, sanction notices, the absence of verifiable reasoning, inconsistent decisions and the concentration of evidentiary trails in the supplier's hands. Absence itself therefore counts as a signal, because the lack of verifiable reasoning and the concentration of trails sit on the same list as the documents that do exist.

Open auditability applies to change communications, the history of relevant versions, confirmation screens, change notices, transaction records, logs sufficient to trace materially relevant interventions, minimum documentation of the supply flow and a minimally intelligible statement of the criteria invoked for relevant reconfigurations.<1>p. 636</1>

The minimum signal of proof appears in the policies applied, sanction notices, the absence of verifiable reasoning, inconsistent decisions and the concentration of evidentiary trails in the supplier's hands, which ties this family directly to the problem of open auditability.<1>p. 672</1>

What is visible, however, does not exhaust what the parameter requires, and gathering this material does not shift to the consumer the burden of reconstructing the supply. The platform holds the complete history of decisions, versions and criteria, while the consumer receives fragments of communication. Auditability cannot depend on whether the consumer happened to keep evidence or has the technical knowledge to put together homemade comparisons.

The platform holds the complete history of decisions, versions and criteria, while the consumer receives only fragments of communication, insufficient to support, in ordinary language, a comparison between the stabilized promise and the reconfigured delivery.<1>p. 471</1>

In a regime where the supplier can update continuously and even automatically, auditability cannot depend on whether the consumer happened to keep evidence or has the technical knowledge to put together homemade comparisons.<1>p. 471</1>
What does the update of an old item show about the auditable minimum?

A technically simple example is the visual effects updates made to old cosmetics in a Riot Games title under the banner of modernization. A cosmetic is an item that changes how a character looks, and in an environment that depends on visual signals and social recognition its value is not exhausted by appearing in the inventory. It includes how the item looks in a match, how clearly it communicates an ability, the visual weight the user experiences and its public distinction from the standard versions. When this set changes persistently, saying that the item is still there does not settle the question, because the core of its utility may have been reconfigured.

In an environment where enjoyment depends on visual signals, legibility and social recognition, the functional value of a cosmetic is not exhausted by its formal presence in the inventory.<1>p. 469</1>
When this set is altered persistently, equivalence is not settled by answering that the item “is still there”, because the core of the utility enjoyed may have been reconfigured.<1>p. 470</1>

Much of the data is public. The Terms of Service provide that the company may use background patches, update packages installed automatically, with or without prior notice. A public text by the company describes the program as an improvement in consistency, legibility and graphic quality and states that its goals are ranked in order of importance, so that gameplay legibility will always prevail over thematic resonance. The result is an institutional decision pattern rather than an isolated event, and none of this disputes the legitimacy of pursuing clarity, which is understandable and, from the ecosystem's point of view, may well be desirable.

The terms further provide that the company may “use background patches” to automatically update games and software “with or without prior notice” <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2024e)</2>.<3>p. 470</3>

In stating its criteria, the text includes ranked goals and a hierarchy of importance, arguing that one of the goals is to “reduce overall visual noise”, for example by “reducing the ‘invasion’ of textures that have many fine and unnecessary details”, and also states that the goals are “ranked in order of importance”, so that “gameplay legibility will always prevail over thematic resonance” <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, 2022a)</2>.<3>p. 470</3>

The point is not to dispute the legitimacy of pursuing clarity, but to recognize that applying these criteria may, in specific cases, reconfigure the core of utility that motivated the purchase of a cosmetic, especially when part of its value lies in the visual experience, in distinction and in the “weight” perceived in game.<1>p. 470</1>

Read against the elements of the auditable minimum, the example shows that compliance may be partial. The stated reason and the criteria exist, and the Patch Notes record changes patch by patch, with titles and dates. That channel serves general information well, but it was not designed as a comparison tool for someone who needs to reconstruct the before and after of a specific cosmetic. What is missing, from the consumer's standpoint, is a stable standard of comparison able to recognize when modernization alters what justified the price and the choice. For such cases there are two ways forward, clearer public criteria for changes or restoration mechanisms as automated as the update itself, which do away with impossible proof when the impact is relevant.

The official “Patch Notes” channel serves as the recurring public record of changes to the game, organized in periodic entries, patch by patch, with titles and dates <1>Riot Games</1><2>(Riot Games, [202-?]b)</2>.<3>p. 471</3>

The format is useful for general information and for minimum communicational transparency, but it is not designed as a tool of comparative auditability for the consumer who needs to reconstruct, technically, the before and after of a specific cosmetic, with objective parameters of demonstration.<1>p. 471</1>

What is missing, from the consumer's standpoint, is a stable standard of comparison able to recognize when modernization alters what justified the price and the choice, especially for items whose value depends on the visual experience and on public distinction.<1>p. 471</1>

If the system does not deliver, as a standard, sufficient comparative elements, the control of functional downgrading requires either clearer public criteria for change or equally automated restoration mechanisms that dispense with impossible proof when the impact is relevant.<1>p. 471</1>

The example calls for a caution, because any cosmetic change falls outside the trigger, and a mere aesthetic preference for an older experience is not enough. A reconciliation is possible through the core that was sold. Changing a cosmetic item is not, by that fact alone, a cosmetic change in that sense, and the case falls within the parameter when part of the value acquired lies in the visual experience and in public distinction. Even so, auditability only prepares the decision. If the change preserves the core of utility, performance goes on. If it significantly downgrades what structured the utility for that consumer, the restoration must include at least mechanisms of choice, such as a refund, credit or exchange for an item of equivalent value, without demanding from the consumer the impossible proof of a black box.
Equivalence is not mere aesthetic preference for an old experience, nor nonconformity with ordinary variations of the service.<1>p. 477</1>

If the change preserves the core of utility, performance goes on. If the change significantly downgrades what structured the utility for that consumer, the restoration must include at least mechanisms of choice that prevent captivity by surprise, with alternatives such as a refund, credit, exchange for another cosmetic of equivalent value or analogous ways of recovering the investment so the consumer can re-enter the ecosystem, without demanding from the consumer the impossible proof of a black box.<1>p. 471</1>

On the sanction side, the case of the irregular gifts, discussed in the chapter on proof, shows the other end of the problem. Once the assets are removed or the account is reverted to an earlier state, what is called a rollback, the user must rely on old statements, scattered emails and screenshots to prove that a given item belonged to their position of enjoyment. In qualified cases, the episode serves as a bridge to open auditability, because the dispute exposes the need for verifiable transparency about the criteria for change, rollback and sanction.

Once the assets are removed or the account is reverted to an earlier state, the user must rely on old statements, scattered emails, past screenshots and reconstructed memory to prove that a given item legitimately belonged to their position of enjoyment.<1>p. 616</1>
On the one hand, to open auditability, because the dispute exposes the need for verifiable transparency about criteria for change, rollback and sanction.<1>p. 617</1>
What happens when the auditable minimum does not come?

The parameter is breached whenever relevant changes in access, performance, utility, operating rules or sanctions affect enjoyment without minimum reconstruction trails being preserved. When the supplier, faced with a relevant change, does not deliver the auditable minimum appropriate to the consumer relationship, its transparency must be treated as inadequate. Depending on the intensity of the case, that inadequacy may serve as evidence or as a direct manifestation of structural abusiveness in the supply regime, so one does not follow automatically from the other. In practice, this legitimizes obligations to act aimed at preserving and producing records, the dynamic redistribution of the burden of proof, presumptions in the consumer's favor when cooperation is refused without justification, and review of the validity or effectiveness of clauses and policies that seek to shield unverifiable changes.

When the supplier, faced with a relevant change, does not provide the auditable minimum appropriate to the consumer relationship, its transparency must be treated as inadequate. And, depending on the intensity of the case, that inadequacy may serve as evidence or as a direct manifestation of structural abusiveness in the supply regime.<1>p. 646</1>

In practice, this legitimizes imposing obligations to act aimed at preserving and producing records, the dynamic redistribution of the burden of proof, the adoption of presumptions in the consumer's favor when cooperation is refused without justification, and review of the validity or effectiveness of clauses and policies that seek to shield unverifiable changes.<1>p. 646</1>
As a matter of remedy, it means that the absence of trails and of verifiability is no longer an operational detail and becomes part of the unlawful act itself.<1>p. 636</1>

The move from parameter to procedure belongs to the chapter on proof, which deals with qualified communication, the minimum documentary core, requests for production of documents, expert examination and the redistribution of the burden. Here it is enough to note the link. The CDC was not designed to let the supplier turn harm into an accounting cost, and it already provides instruments suited to production of documents, early production of evidence and specific relief. Bruno Miragem stresses the primacy of specific performance and of actions for production of documents. Without access to the versions, the performance records and the evidence of what was actually supplied, the discussion is held hostage by the base contract, which often says little about how the service really works.
The CDC was not designed to allow the supplier to turn the harm into a mere accounting cost and move on.<1>p. 645</1>

Without access to the relevant versions, the performance records and the elements showing what was actually supplied, the legal discussion risks being held hostage by the documentary fiction of the base contract, which often says little about the real life of the service<1>p. 646</1>

Specific performance of the obligation takes precedence precisely to keep the supplier from turning nonperformance into an advantageous economic calculation, treating harms converted into damages as an ordinary cost of doing business. Conversion into compensation should therefore occur only at the consumer's option or when specific relief or an equivalent practical result is impossible <1>Miragem</1><2>(Miragem, 2020, p. 898)</2>.<3>p. 646</3>

This framework works together with preliminary measures for the early production of evidence, notably actions for production of documents, especially in disputes where the contract was never delivered to the consumer or where the actual content of the relationship must be reconstructed <1>Miragem</1><2>(Miragem, 2020, p. 903)</2>.<3>p. 646</3>
All the mechanisms answer the same requirement: to keep the supplier's exclusive technical control from becoming a monopoly over the proof of the very unlawful act alleged.<1>p. 663</1>

Auditability alone does not decide whether a change is materially legitimate, because showing what changed does not answer whether the change preserved the substance of the enjoyment acquired. That second question belongs to functional value equivalence, which has a chapter of its own. Each criterion presupposes the other, since without auditability equivalence is hard to prove, and without equivalence auditability risks becoming a mere ability to narrate changes. In short, one governs the how of the mutation and the other the how much and the what, and this yields two tests for the interpreter. The first asks whether there was minimum institutional verifiability, with reasoning, timing, effects and reconstruction trails. The second asks whether the change preserved sufficient functional equivalence or significantly downgraded the practical and symbolic core of the object. The order matters, because the change is reconstructed first and its legitimacy measured afterward. When one test fails, the change becomes legally suspect, and when both fail, the case comes very close to a supply defect, an abusive practice, a breach of trust or an architecture of structural opacity.

On its own, open auditability does not resolve the whole dispute, because demonstrating what changed and how it changed does not exhaust the question of the material legitimacy of the change.<1>p. 647</1>
One standard controls the how of the mutation; the other, the how much and the what of the mutation.<1>p. 638</1>

First, was there minimum institutional verifiability of the change, with reasoning, timing, effects and trails for reconstructing the supply? Second, did the change preserve sufficient functional equivalence with the enjoyment legitimately acquired, or did it significantly downgrade the practical and symbolic core of the object?<1>p. 639</1>
First, the change is reconstructed. Then, its material legitimacy is measured. This order matters. Without it, the supplier will always have the advantage of the fog.<1>p. 647</1>

When one of these conditions fails, the legitimacy of the change already becomes legally suspect. When both fail at once, the case comes very close to a supply defect, an abusive practice, a breach of trust or even an architecture of structural opacity incompatible with the consumer protection regime.<1>p. 638-639</1>
Doesn't auditing mean disclosing trade secrets?

The first is the secrecy objection, which holds that requiring auditability would mean opening the code, handing over trade secrets and stripping the software of protection. The answer is that the legal order already accommodates limited forms of scrutiny that preserve the informational asset, such as sealed proceedings, restricted expert access, narrowly defined functional analysis and institutional oversight. Denis Borges Barbosa notes that sealing a case restricts third-party access to sensitive information, such as source code, and bars the opposing party from using it for purposes unrelated to the dispute. Reconciling protection of the asset with the need for verification is therefore nothing new.
The protection of software does not turn it into a sacred black box.<1>p. 643</1>

This point is important because the business objection usually comes in predictable guise: requiring auditability would amount to requiring the opening of code, the surrender of trade secrets, the exposure of know-how or the stripping of the software's protection.<1>p. 643</1>

Sealed proceedings, restricted expert access, narrowly defined functional analysis, technically necessary use for certain purposes and institutional oversight do not demolish exclusivity.<1>p. 643</1>

The legal framework itself provides for sealed proceedings, which restrict third-party access to sensitive information, such as source code, and bar the opposing party from using it for purposes unrelated to the dispute <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2017, p. 1940)</2>.<3>p. 643</3>

A secret also has to be shown in order to be protected. Invoking secrecy or technical sensitivity in general terms, without specifying what must remain confidential, is not enough, and Barbosa observes that judicial control requires identifying what the secret is, because a broad assertion that it relates to the company's line of business makes such control impossible. The protection remains legitimate, but what matters to Consumer Law is not, as a rule, the internal ingenuity of the program, but how a given operating regime, change or criterion affected enjoyment. The examination concerns how the system functions, for purposes of oversight, and not the parasitic appropriation of the asset. When technical decisions make continued use of the service depend on invasive requirements, the need for the platform not to hide behind technical opacity and trade secrets becomes all the stronger.
The company can still protect its secret. What it cannot do is claim secrecy over the very impact of the change it imposed on the consumer.<1>p. 644</1>

Invoking “secrecy” or “technical sensitivity” in general terms, without specifying what actually needs to remain confidential and without allowing any institutionally relevant form of reconstruction, is not enough.<1>p. 644</1>
For confidentiality to be legally respected, it needs to be identified and carved out, not treated as a magic fog that dissolves every requirement of accountability.<1>p. 644</1>

For the matter to be subject to judicial control, “it is necessary to unveil and identify what secret would have been disclosed”, and it is not enough to allege broadly that it is a secret related to the company's line of business, because so sweeping an assertion does not allow effective judicial control of the dispute <1>Barbosa</1><2>(Barbosa, 2018, p. 392)</2>.<3>p. 644</3>
The legally relevant examination concerns how the system functions, for purposes of oversight, not the parasitic appropriation of the asset.<1>p. 644</1>

When technical decisions and internal policies extend the extraterritorial reach of code, making continued use and participation depend on invasive requirements or on control mechanisms that go beyond the perimeter of the contracted object, they reveal a claim to practical sovereignty over the consumer and the consumer's material means, which reinforces the need for open auditability as a minimum requirement so that the platform does not hide behind technical opacity and trade secrets, and so that governance by architecture is treated as conduct that is imputable, contestable and subject to proportionality.<1>p. 499</1>

The second is the objection of technical complexity. Without the parameter, the supplier can always claim that it made the change for technical reasons, that it gave what information it could, that the impact was small, that the change was provided for in some document and that the consumer simply did not understand or did not like it. With the parameter, one can ask what was changed, on what basis, with what effect and with what reconstruction trails. A generic appeal to internal policy, security, service improvement or ecosystem integrity is not a self-sufficient justification, and legitimate complexity is not the same as obscurity used as a technique of power.
In continuous consumer relationships, complexity does not revoke good faith.<1>p. 647</1>

Without this standard, the supplier can always claim that it made the change for technical reasons, that it gave what information it could, that the impact was small, that the change was provided for in some document and that the consumer simply did not understand or did not like it.<1>p. 645</1>

On the other, it keeps a generic appeal to “internal policy”, “security”, “service improvement” or “ecosystem integrity” from serving as a self-sufficient justification immune to control, which would hollow out the duties of information, loyalty and adequacy in continuing performance.<1>p. 473</1>
In governed environments, this is what separates legitimate complexity from obscurity functionalized as a technique of power.<1>p. 728</1>

The third is that the requirement would multiply technical litigation. The opposite is true, because the parameter serves to contain disputes. With preserved trails, identifiable versions and reasons that can be stated, it avoids an endless war of opaque technicalities, in which each side speaks a different language and the decision ends up resting on intuitive deference to the better organized party. Expert examinations, production of documents and orders to clarify then bear on knowable objects, and the dispute stays within bounds.
Open auditability also serves to contain litigation.<1>p. 728</1>

When there are preserved trails, identifiable relevant versions, reasons for change that can at least minimally be stated and basic elements for reconstructing the conflict, the court case is kept from turning into an endless war of opaque technicalities, in which each side speaks a different language and the decision ends up resting on intuitive deference to the better organized party.<1>p. 728</1>

The fourth is that the parameter invents a right or stifles innovation. On invention, besides its roots in the duty to inform, there is support in Karl Larenz, who describes the legal system as open and, to a certain degree, mobile, so the two operators do not replace the system but let it see, through controllable criteria, what shorthand formulas tend to erase. On innovation, the answer is that auditability is a criterion for the legitimacy of platform architectures, not hostility toward them. Platforms may innovate, update, fix, rebalance, migrate and protect their technical assets. What they cannot do is any of this under a regime of institutional irreconstructibility.

Larenz describes the system as an “‘open’ system and, to a certain degree, a ‘mobile’ one”, always incomplete and continually put into question, whose function is to make clear the “intrinsic rationality”, the guiding values and the principles of Law <1>Larenz</1><2>(Larenz, 1997, p. 241)</2>.<3>p. 481</3>

Open auditability and functional value equivalence occupy this place: they do not replace the system; they allow it to see, through controllable criteria, what shorthand formulas tend to erase.<1>p. 481</1>

Open auditability must therefore be understood as a criterion for the legitimacy of platform architectures, and not as abstract hostility toward them. Platforms may innovate, update, fix, rebalance, migrate and protect their technical assets. What they cannot do is any of this under a regime of institutional irreconstructibility, as if the very complexity of the system entitled them to decide alone what matters, what was changed and what may or may not be known by those who enjoy the service and by those who oversee it legally.<1>p. 647</1>
What does open auditability not reach?

The name calls for careful reading. Open auditability does not require total transparency, unrestricted opening of the infrastructure, or disclosure of source code, the full architecture of the system or sensitive trade secrets, nor full disclosure of proprietary models and metrics. Nor does it require absolute explainability or technical omniscience on the part of the judge, and the platform remains the owner of its intangible assets and internal architecture. Anyone who frames the claim as a sweeping search of the system is asking for something the parameter does not provide.

The name must be read carefully to avoid misunderstanding. It is not about requiring the opening of code, a sweeping search of the infrastructure, full disclosure of internal systems or theatrical laboratory transparency.<1>p. 636</1>

This is not a requirement of total transparency, nor of unrestricted opening of the technical infrastructure, nor an obligation to disclose source code, the full architecture of the system or sensitive trade secrets.<1>p. 640</1>
Its aim is neither to make the technical and organizational environment fully transparent nor to require full disclosure of models, source code, proprietary metrics or trade secrets.<1>p. 472</1>
The parameter is calibrated precisely to make control possible without demanding technical omniscience from the judge or disrupting the economic functioning of the ecosystem.<1>p. 728</1>

The platform remains the owner of its intangible assets and internal architecture, but can no longer invoke them to block entirely the institutional reconstruction of events that affect the consumer's enjoyment in a legally relevant way.<1>p. 729</1>

As to which changes it reaches, the parameter leaves out microscopic adjustments, cosmetic changes and irrelevant fluctuations, and it does not turn every update into litigation. Not every change is unlawful, and not every improvement becomes a problem, because updates may be needed for compatibility, security, stability and legibility. As to effects, a lack of auditability makes the change legally suspect, and inadequate transparency amounts to structural abusiveness only depending on the intensity of the case. What the parameter provides is a basis for reconstruction, which does not dispense with the material examination of equivalence.
This problem does not turn every improvement into an unlawful act. Updates may be necessary for compatibility, security, stability and legibility in a competitive ecosystem.<1>p. 470</1>
The section, then, does not turn every change into an unlawful act. It simply refuses to let change become an automatic alibi for irresponsibility.<1>p. 639</1>

What remains after these exclusions is a minimum the supplier cannot refuse without consequences. Business secrecy, economic exclusivity and the complexity of the service no longer operate as absolute vetoes and become factors to be reconciled with duties of minimum verifiability. Opacity is no longer a zone naturally immune to legal protection and becomes a legal problem that can be handled through preservation orders, narrowly defined production of documents, restricted expert examination and verifiable reasoning. The service can still change, but not beyond legal control, and private governance no longer edges toward practical sovereignty.
Technical opacity, by itself, does not work as a free zone of liability.<1>p. 481</1>

Business secrecy, economic exclusivity and the complexity of the service no longer operate as absolute vetoes on control and become factors to be reconciled with duties of minimum verifiability.<1>p. 728-729</1>

Structural opacity thus ceases to be a zone naturally immune to legal protection and becomes a legal problem that can be handled through preservation orders, narrowly defined production of documents, restricted expert examination, verifiable reasoning and other instruments consistent with the procedural and administrative rationality of the protective system.<1>p. 729</1>
Without this standard, private governance comes too close to practical sovereignty. With it, the mutability of the service remains possible, but no longer hovers above legal control.<1>p. 648</1>
