The protected goods

The protected goods are what the harm reaches when the platform lowers, sanctions or erases the position of enjoyment of an Immaterial Object of Consumption, even when formal access remains open, and they go by the names of personal integrity, symbolic identity and biographical continuity. They are defined by public criteria and are linked to civil personality, which is why losing a history or a title may go beyond losing an item.
What is lost when access remains open?

In platform-governed ecosystems, what the consumer keeps over time is more than access to a digital performance. It is a position of enjoyment that incorporates history, memory, recognition, identity projection and continuity of presence in the environment. That is why certain losses, erasures, sanctions and unilateral reconfigurations reach beyond the economic value of the purchase, extending to dimensions of personal integrity and symbolic identity. The problem is to define these losses so that they are neither downgraded to mere displeasure nor treated as a side effect of the service.

In digital ecosystems, the value offered and enjoyed is not exhausted by instrumental utilities, because it depends on regimes of visibility, recognition, belonging and reputation that are part of the very experience of enjoyment and condition the subject's practical position in the environment.<1>p. 456-457</1>

In platform-governed ecosystems, what the consumer keeps over time is not only functional access to a digital performance, but a position of enjoyment that incorporates history, memory, recognition, identity projection and practical continuity of presence in the environment.<1>p. 534</1>

The corresponding legal protection, therefore, cannot be blind to the circumstance that certain losses, erasures, sanctions and unilateral reconfigurations reach not only the economic value of the acquisition, but also dimensions of personal integrity and symbolic identity that become objectified in the very course of the digital experience.<1>p. 534</1>

The difficulty lies in the shape of the harm, which does not always appear as a total interruption. Access may remain nominal while the experience is degraded by persistent changes in the conditions of participation, predictability and governability of the environment, and it is precisely these losses, which reach the enjoyment bundle without interrupting the service, that protection needs to cover. Protection thus no longer depends on the crude figure of total interruption.

Protection ceases to depend on the crude figure of total interruption and extends to situations in which access remains nominal, but the experience of use is lowered by persistent changes in the conditions of participation, predictability and governability of the environment.<1>p. 458</1>

The problem is to make them legally treatable through objective delimitations and criteria of controllability, including so as to capture losses that reach the enjoyment bundle even when there is no total interruption, but rather a persistent lowering of the conditions of use and recognition.<1>p. 457</1>
Why does neither price nor feeling measure this loss?

The common reading goes wrong in two directions. On one side is the patrimonialist view, which confines the problem to the value of the good affected and turns every conflict into price and residual compensation, a view that does not hold up against Anderson Schreiber, for whom rereading private law in light of human dignity requires attention to the existential projections of the person. On the other side is the reading that treats symbolic value as a private emotional projection and therefore as legally irrelevant, and it fails too, because part of the value enjoyed in these environments is symbolic and socially structured.

The rereading of private law in light of human dignity broke long ago with the narrow view that confined the legal problem to the patrimonial value of the good affected, requiring attention to the existential projections of the person in the social world <1>Schreiber</1><2>(Schreiber, 2014, p. 10; p. 17)</2>.<3>p. 534</3>

Protection ceases to operate under an institutional blindness that converts every conflict into price and residual compensation and comes to admit, on the basis of the system itself, remedies of functional restoration, preservation of trails, access to records, procedural correction and restoration of the position of enjoyment whenever this is possible and legally due.<1>p. 543</1>

The progression of the argument then requires making explicit that part of the value enjoyed in digital ecosystems is not only instrumental, but symbolic and socially structured. To that end, it is necessary to set aside the reading that symbolic value is a mere private emotional projection, immune to control and, for that reason, legally irrelevant.<1>p. 459</1>

The way out is not to swap price for feeling. The point is not to dissolve the analysis into sentimentalism. The question is more sober, because in platform environments the consumer's personality is broken down into data, profiles, histories, metrics, reputations and participation trails. Following Schreiber, the harm is understood through the attribute of personality objectively affected, and not through the suffering subjectively experienced, which keeps protection from depending on sentimental proof or on a dramatization of the harm.

In platform environments, the consumer's personality is cut into data, profiles, histories, metrics, reputations and participation trails that condition concrete possibilities of permanence, recognition and self-determination.<1>p. 535</1>

This does not mean dissolving the analysis into academic sentimentalism, an elegant shortcut for thinking ill of the one whose conduct is now being questioned. The question at hand is more sober.<1>p. 535</1>

When records, signs, usage trajectories, digital historicity and symbolic belongings come to structure objectifiable forms of personal continuity, the corresponding impact no longer fits comfortably in the narrow grammar of the lost price. This key becomes even clearer when the harm is understood not from the suffering subjectively experienced, but from the attribute of personality objectively affected. The advantage of this formulation lies precisely in preventing the protection of the person from depending on sentimental proof or on dramatization of the harm, concentrating instead on the legally protected projection that was violated <1>Schreiber</1><2>(Schreiber, 2014, p. 17)</2>.<3>p. 534-535</3>

The methodological basis comes from Miguel Reale and Tércio Sampaio Ferraz Jr. Reale describes the norm as an integration of facts and values, and it is this integration that allows governed enjoyment to be treated as a legally modelable experience. Reale also observes that an unforeseen technical circumstance may alter the meaning and content of a legal text. Ferraz Jr. supplies the safeguard, because dogmatic delimitation works by cutting into reality to isolate the problems relevant to the decision, and dogmatics can deal with this kind of loss only if it is able to make it decidable without falling into descriptive paralysis.

The legal norm operates as an integration between facts and values, without being reduced to an empty logical form and without being confused with a mechanical reflection of the world. It is this integration that authorizes treating platform-governed enjoyment as a legally modelable experience<1>p. 457</1>

In scenarios of technical mutation, legal meaning may shift without the answer depending on moral rhetoric, since “an unforeseen circumstance of a technical order may completely alter the meaning and content of a legal text” <1>Reale</1><2>(Reale, 2001, p. 164)</2>.<3>p. 457</3>

Dogmatics, however, only operates with this kind of loss if it is capable of carving out the phenomenon and making it decidable, avoiding descriptive paralysis in the face of the complexity of the environment. Under the technological function already established, the dogmatic cut operates by a cut in reality that isolates the problems relevant to decision-making <1>Jr.</1><2>(Ferraz Jr., 2003, [p. 92])</2> and organizes uncertainties into a specialized technique compatible with normative binding and with the institutional pressure for decision <3>Jr.</3><4>(Ferraz Jr., 2003, [p. 86-87])</4>.<5>p. 458</5>
Why do the protected goods appear under different names?

The protected goods do not go by a single name. At the opening of the part devoted to the regime of the IOC, two complementary dimensions appear, functional integrity, linked to performance and to the utility delivered, and symbolic integrity, linked to belonging, reputation, distinction and promises of identity. Shortly afterward, the two are gathered under the name of personal integrity, a category with two articulated faces. In its own section, personal integrity becomes an umbrella concept and symbolic identity appears as a distinct category. In the typology of digitally based business models, the pair returns as functional integrity and symbolic identity, and in the part on the constitutional order biographical continuity joins them.
The identity and symbolic face protects belonging, reputation, distinction and the promise of recognition mediated by signs of the environment.<1>p. 395</1>

The decisive point is that, in platform ecosystems, the object does not present itself as a stabilized thing, but as a bundle of functional and symbolic enjoyment that depends on regimes of access, visibility, updating and governance. For this reason, adequate protection requires recognizing two complementary dimensions. Functional integrity, linked to performance, to the conditions of use and to the utility actually delivered. And symbolic integrity, linked to belonging, reputation, distinction and promises of identity mediated by signs and internal equivalences of the environment, when these elements are part of the performance as offered and perceived.<1>p. 391</1>

Next, personal integrity is introduced to name the legal goods whose erosion constitutes the relevant harm. It is a category with two faces that operate in articulation, and not as separate categories. The functional face protects performance, use and the utility actually delivered.<1>p. 395</1>

Functional integrity and symbolic identity delimit the field of relevant losses beyond binary interruption, reaching degradations of enjoyment and disorganizations of the sign-value associated with belonging, distinction and recognition.<1>p. 483</1>
The protected core of enjoyment comes to include personal integrity and symbolic identity, objectified in history, reputation, memory, belonging and continuity of trajectory.<1>p. 543</1>

The shifting names do not undo the content. Protection covers the functional integrity of the acquired object and the personal and symbolic integrity of the consumer. Measured against the doctrine of digital goods, the regime seeks protection of using and, in certain cases, protection of being, whenever enjoyment incorporates symbolic identity and biographical continuity. Both formulations describe a constant pair, what the object does for the consumer and who the consumer is within the environment. The second pole changes name with the angle of view and becomes biographical continuity when the focus falls on time. In the two-faces formulation, personal integrity covers both poles. In the umbrella formulation, it adds to the classic integrities a facet of agency that serves both to exercise use and to exist in the system, and symbolic identity stands beside it, linked by the two captivities.

To make this phenomenon legally visible, the category of Immaterial Object of Consumption (IOC) is proposed as an infrastructure-concept capable of giving concrete form to the notion of immaterial product provided for in art. 3, § 1, of the Consumer Protection Code<1><2>1</2></1> as a governed enjoyment bundle. Under this formulation, legal protection no longer focuses only on the formal regularity of the performance and extends to the functional integrity of the acquired object and the personal and symbolic integrity of the consumer.<3>p. 11</3>

The regime of the IOC takes on the civil-law gain, rejects the strawman of the legal nonexistence of the digital and repositions the debate on the ground that matters. It seeks the protection of using, the control of functional integrity and, in certain cases, the protection of being, whenever enjoyment incorporates the symbolic identity and biographical continuity of the consumer user.<1>p. 573-574</1>

The two faces need to be thought of together because the enjoyment of the IOC is not realized by separating one from the other, and because the relevant degradation of continuous consumption usually falls simultaneously on both, as happens when a unilateral reconfiguration preserves technical access but lowers the reputational or symbolic position of the consumer in the ecosystem.<1>p. 395</1>

For anyone building a claim, the practical consequence is that no new legal good is created. Using personal integrity as an umbrella is an operation that engages with the settled dogmatics of the CDC, and identity captivity does not create a new good either, because its relevance lies in making a specific form of loss in the fact of consumption controllable. In either formulation, what decides is the description of the loss by verifiable criteria, not the label chosen.

The use of “personal integrity” as an umbrella concept to encompass the pairing “health and safety” native to consumer protection does not propose the creation of a new legal good, but an operation that engages directly with the dogmatics already settled in the CDC.<1>p. 465</1>

In consumer-law terms, the relevance of the concept is not to create a new good, but to make controllable a specific form of loss in the fact of consumption, in which the integrity of agency and symbolic identity are corroded by instability, opacity and manufactured risk, affecting the adequacy of the regime of enjoyment and the legitimate trust that sustains continuous platform-governed relationships.<1>p. 225</1>
What does personal integrity protect?

Personal integrity is defined negatively and positively. It does not designate an emotional state or discomfort in the face of the ordinary frustrations of the market, but the preservation of minimum conditions of agency, continuity and practical orientation of the consumer in an environment that permanently administers the possibilities of enjoyment. In this environment, the consumer participates in an ecosystem that organizes access, priorities, visibilities and sanctions. Integrity is affected when these conditions are lowered persistently or structurally, to the point of turning use into chronic instability, functional disorientation or loss of control over one's own way of existing in the environment, even if formal access remains available.

The legal relevance, therefore, lies not in measuring internal shocks, but in identifying when the continuous administration of the environment significantly alters the level of predictability, consistency and governability of enjoyment, corroding the core of utility stabilized in the relationship.<1>p. 458</1>

Personal integrity, in the regime of the Immaterial Object of Consumption, does not designate an emotional state or subjective discomfort arising from ordinary frustrations of the market. It designates the preservation of minimum conditions of agency, continuity and practical orientation of the consumer within a technical-organizational environment that permanently administers the possibilities of enjoyment. When the acquired utility is realized as a position of enjoyment sustained by a platform, the subject is not only the recipient of content, but a participant in an ecosystem that organizes access, priorities, visibilities and sanctions.<1>p. 457</1>

Integrity is affected when these conditions are lowered persistently or structurally, to the point of turning the experience of use into chronic instability, functional disorientation or loss of control over one's own way of existing in the environment, even if formal access remains available.<1>p. 458</1>

The umbrella has two layers of content. The first is that of the classic integrities, physical, psychic, patrimonial and even aesthetic. The second is a facet specific to continuous consumption, integrity of the capacity for agency and predictability, understood as the minimum set of conditions that allows consumers to orient their own action, understand practical consequences, plan their continued presence and exercise use according to stabilizable expectations. Nor does this facet correspond to an emotional state or to a psychological standard of protection, because it designates a functional condition of existence in the system, observable in the governability of the environment, the stability of the rules and the legibility of consequences.

For this impact to be legally assimilable, it is necessary to make explicit the content of what is understood here by personal integrity in the regime of the IOC. The term is used as an umbrella concept compatible with the theory of quality in the CDC, which already operates through categories broad enough to encompass harms arising from the fact of consumption without requiring the crude figure of total interruption or of immediate material injury.<1>p. 465</1>

Personal integrity includes, therefore, classic dimensions of physical, psychic, patrimonial and even aesthetic integrity, but now also comes to incorporate an operational facet proper to continuous consumption in an environment. It is integrity as to the capacity for agency and predictability, understood as a minimum set of conditions that allows the consumer to orient his own action, understand practical consequences, plan permanence and exercise use according to stabilizable normative expectations in an ecosystem governed by architecture and by private sanctions. This integrity of agency does not correspond to a private emotional state or to a psychological parameter of protection. It designates a functional condition of existence in the system, observable in patterns of governability of the environment, of stability of rules and of legibility of consequences.<1>p. 465-466</1>

The grounding in Consumer Law comes from Claudia Lima Marques. In her reconstruction, consumer protection is organized at least around the protection of physical-psychic integrity and economic integrity, and the CDC's theory of quality operates through the legal duty of quality-adequacy and quality-safety. The agency facet may thus be presented as an extension of the adequacy of the supply regime itself, and not as a normative innovation. Julie E. Cohen explains why this facet belongs to the supply, arguing that networked information technologies do not merely empower the connected subject but configure it, so that agency comes to be treated as a governable variable of the service.

In Claudia Lima Marques's reconstruction, consumer protection in the market is organized, at least, by the protection of the consumer's physical-psychic integrity and economic integrity, in addition to the concern with the moment at which this protection applies in the contractual dynamics <1>Marques</1><2>(Marques, 2016, p. 13)</2>. This framework engages directly with the theory of quality in the CDC, understood as a legal duty of quality-adequacy and quality-safety, by which defects of inadequacy and of insecurity are qualified according to reasonable expectations of supply, functionally replacing the classic categories of the latent defect in the previous regime <3>Marques</3><4>(Marques, 2016, p. 1349)</4>. Within this framing, the inclusion of an operational facet linked to agency and predictability in environments of platform-governed enjoyment may be presented as an extension of the adequacy of the supply regime itself, and not as a normative innovation.<5>p. 465</5>

Personal integrity and symbolic identity become fully intelligible as dimensions of the IOC when it is recognized that, in platform-governed environments, agency and identity are not located outside the supply as mere psychological phenomena, but may be configured by architectural design and by continuous modulation. Cohen synthesizes this point by stating that technologies and artifacts mediate the embodied perception of reality and that, over time, they come to constitute and define the lived world, so that networked information technologies do not merely empower the networked self, but configure it <1>Cohen</1><2>(Cohen, 2012, [p. 36])</2>.<3>p. 463</3>

The legal consequence is that agency comes to be treated as a governable variable of the supply and that motivational patterns may be reinforced in pre-deliberative layers by techniques of choice architecture and algorithmic anticipation <1>Cohen</1><2>(Cohen, 2019, p. 77)</2>.<3>p. 463</3>
How is personal integrity linked to civil personality?

In the part on the constitutional order, personal integrity gains an informational and biographical dimension, because people also come to project themselves socially through their digital records, their accumulated trajectory and their recognizable position in the ecosystem. Danilo Doneda treats data, records, profiles and histories as a direct representation of personality and, to some extent, as its extension in the digital environment. Canavez and coauthors recognize digital dossiers as a new type of identity. It follows that erasures, blocks, resets, which are redefinitions of progress, and suppressions of trajectory cannot automatically be reduced to simple patrimonial loss.

This key makes it possible to formulate, in more rigorous terms, the idea of personal integrity in the consumption of IOCs. It is not exhausted in physical or psychic integrity in the classic sense, but reaches informational and biographical integrity, because the subject comes to project himself socially also through his digital records, his accumulated trajectory and his recognizable position in the ecosystem.<1>p. 535</1>

Data, records, profiles and histories are not only economically exploitable informational collections; they work as a direct representation of personality and, to some extent, as its extension in the digital environment <1>Doneda</1><2>(Doneda, 2020, p. 146-147; p. 149)</2>.<3>p. 535</3>

In contemporary terms, it means recognizing that so-called digital dossiers constitute a new type of identity and that personal data are connected to the free exercise and development of the human personality <1>Laprano</1><2>(Canavez; Andrade; Laprano, 2021, p. 141; p. 153)</2>. Consequently, erasures, blocks, resets and suppressions of trajectory cannot be automatically reduced to a mere, simple patrimonial loss.<3>p. 535-536</3>

There is also a classic grounding. Warren and Brandeis showed that the law needed to recognize thoughts, emotions, sensations and other immaterial forms of existence, not on the exclusive basis of property, but on the broader notion of inviolate personality. Schreiber completes the picture by explaining that reputation, honor and identity receive protection because they are part of objective relational dimensions of the person's life, and not because they are intimate feelings, and Mariana Monteiro da Costa adds that data protection needs to consider the subject's physical and electronic body. The digital environment is thus also a space of identity projection.
The digital environment, in short, is not only a market; it is also a space of identity projection and of existential incidence.<1>p. 539</1>

The old formulation of Warren and Brandeis is useful here precisely because it shows that the law, over time, needed to recognize that thoughts, emotions, sensations and other immaterial forms of existence also call for legal protection, not on the exclusive basis of property, but on the broader idea of inviolate personality <1>Brandeis</1><2>(Warren; Brandeis, [201-?], [p. 2-3; p. 10])</2>.<3>p. 536</3>

The civil protection of personality reaches precisely the way in which the person is projected, recognized and situated in the social milieu, which is why reputation, honor and identity receive protection not because they are mere intimate feelings, but because they are part of objective relational dimensions of the person's life <1>Schreiber</1><2>(Schreiber, 2014, p. 71; p. 211)</2>.<3>p. 537-538</3>
Data protection needs to consider the subject's physical and electronic body, and not only the abstract circulation of information <1>Costa</1><2>(Costa, 2018, p. 41; p. 44; p. 47)</2>.<3>p. 538</3>

The link with personality has an express limit. In consumer law, the argument needs to keep its feet on the ground, and the limit comes from Marques. In relationships of vulnerability, dependence and continued trust, the rebalancing that can be required must extend to fair and dignified treatment and protect expectations that go beyond the economic account. Reale supplies the axiological basis by treating the inviolability of the human person as a value that, once brought to historical consciousness, comes to be considered intangible, and when values of this kind appear as conditions of the system itself, valuation takes the form of a limit, not of rhetoric. Along the same line, in qualified cases, the loss of an account, a history or a trajectory may constitute moral damages for injury to personality, a matter for the chapter on remedies.

On the consumer plane, the argument needs to keep its feet on the ground. Contractual and consumer protection is not exhausted in the control of price nor in the restoration of narrow patrimonial imbalances. What is symbolic identity, and how is it demonstrated?

Symbolic identity is the public position of the consumer in a platform-administered ecosystem of signs, in which visibility, reputation, belonging and distinction work as practical conditions of enjoyment. It is formed by criteria of recognition almost always encoded in metrics, badges, rarities, rankings, participation history and access regimes. When the utility of the object depends on these mediations, the enjoyment bundle includes the continuity of this position, and the platform may keep access to the content open and still degrade the position by reconfiguring the criteria of status and recognition.

Symbolic identity, in the regime of the IOC, designates the public position of the consumer in a platform-administered ecosystem of signs, in which visibility, reputation, belonging and distinction work as practical conditions of enjoyment and as components of the economically experienced value.<1>p. 459</1>

This identity is formed and stabilized by socially operative criteria of recognition, often encoded in metrics, badges, rarities, rankings, participation history, relationship networks and regimes of access to spaces and features. When the utility of the object depends on these mediations, the enjoyment bundle structurally includes the continuity of this position and the possibility of exercising it over time.<1>p. 459</1>

The platform may formally preserve access to the content and, even so, reconfigure the criteria that define status, reach, belonging and recognition, degrading the socially instituted core of utility that sustained enjoyment as a practice.<1>p. 459</1>

What keeps this notion from turning into introspection is the semiotic lock. Following Umberto Eco, the sign is understood as a public structure that organizes conduct and produces verifiable social effects, and interpretation as an objective fact, because relations of interpretation do not necessarily depend on individual mental representations and are collectively verifiable. Meaning operates as a relation instituted by the code, and even connotation becomes predictable through a shared lexicon, which allows symbolic losses to be described by public criteria. The chapter on equivalence shows how this same lock enters the comparison between an item before and after a change.
